title: a scripture that is the guru
hook: a scripture that is the Guru; why it's carried, covered, put to bed

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guru Gobind Singh. Your line was sword and saint. Today, who he named to come after him. Day twenty.

Late evening at a gurdwara. The last hymn has been sung. Someone gently closes a very large book, wraps it in embroidered cloth, and lifts it onto their head. Someone else waves a whisk of long white hair over it, the way attendants once did for a king. It's carried to its own room, laid on a bed and covered for the night. At dawn it's carried back out and opened, and the day begins. Why would anyone put a book to bed?
screen: `A LARGE BOOK, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `PUT TO BED FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means book. Sahib is a word of deep respect. And Guru, the teacher from day one. The Guru who is a book. Here's how that happened. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him and his own, and in 1604 installed the collection at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Then, in 1708, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh declared there would be no more human Gurus. From then on, Sikhs would find their Guru in the scripture. So when Sikhs bow before it, they aren't bowing to paper and ink. They're bowing to the Guru, present in the words. That's why it's treated like a revered teacher in the room: higher than everyone, under a canopy, attended with a whisk, put to rest at night. And inside? Hymns by six of the Gurus, and, remarkably, by holy poets who weren't Sikhs at all: Kabir, a weaver; Ravidas, from a caste many looked down on; Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. Almost all of it is poetry, arranged by musical mode, meant to be sung. Every morning, gurdwaras open it and read the first hymn on the page as the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs don't only read this book. They listen to it.
screen: `GRANTH — BOOK. SAHIB — RESPECT.` · `1708: NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `TREATED LIKE A TEACHER IN THE ROOM.` · `GURUS AND SAINTS, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of words that have spoken to you: a line from a book, a letter, something someone once said that you've never forgotten. Bring it to mind as exactly as you can. Now imagine those words not as print, but as someone sitting beside you, saying them to you now. Let them speak, and just listen.
The Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru since 1708, holding the Gurus' hymns and the words of other saints. Twentieth word.
Your line: a living book. Read as if someone were speaking to you today. Day twenty.

howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy on a raised platform, is attended with a chaur, opened at dawn and put to rest at night; a hymn read each morning is taken as the day's hukamnama.

fork.setup: you're the tenth Guru, near the end of your life. who comes after you?
options: your chosen successor, the eleventh Guru.
the scripture itself, as the Guru.
fork.reveal: Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the Guru. that's why Sikhs bow to it, and why it's put to rest at night.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: guru (teacher) + granth (book) + sahib (a word of deep respect).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikh holy book.
what it means: the Guru itself, present in the words: honored like a living teacher, carried, covered and put to rest.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604; the final form adds the hymns of the ninth Guru. it runs to 1,430 angs, arranged by raga.

sources.ref: Sikh history on the Adi Granth (1604) and Guru Gobind Singh's declaration (1708)

notes: Ravidas described as 'from a caste many looked down on'; confirm wording is respectful.
The chaur is compared to the whisk once waved for a king; confirm.

Hukamnama described as reading the first hymn on the page (the practice is to open at random and read the hymn beginning at the top of the left-hand page, or continuing from before). Confirm the simplification.
Six Gurus' hymns (Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Tegh Bahadur); confirm.
Research: 'why do Sikhs bow to a book?' is a common questioning-stage question; the teach now answers it in one line (bowing to the Guru present in the words, not paper and ink). Confirm.
